title: AC Patterns
subject: gated-scoped-ac
summary: **What.** The patterns a service or repository uses to call the engine for each CRUD operation. One pattern per (operation × execution target).

claims.text: Every storage operation is authorized through the engine.
Authorization narrows reachable rows and accessible fields.
Reads narrow at the repository; writes gate at the service.
A write against a specific row passes that row's identity through the engine's filter — by submission (create) or by repository confirmation (update, delete).
Every authorization decision is observable.
**Why.** Without a fixed pattern per operation, every developer rediscovers when to call which `resolve*` method, where to gate, and what to log. Drift produces silent over- or under-permission.

**How.** Reads narrow the result set inside the repository; writes gate before executing inside the service. Each operation has between one and two gates depending on whether the row's full identity is known up-front.

**Why this way.** Reads need narrowing, not a yes/no — narrowing is the result. Writes need a yes/no, not narrowing — and that yes/no must include any field of the target row the rules reference. The two-gate pattern for update/delete is the only way to answer "can this user touch *this* row" when the rule conditions on fields the caller didn't submit.

reference.statement: **What.** The patterns a service or repository uses to call the engine for each CRUD operation. One pattern per (operation × execution target).

imagesAndDiagrams.value:
| Operation | Execution target | Gates | Where they live | Engine call |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Create** | Repository (internal) | 1 | Service | `engine.resolveCreate(roles, entity, subjects, properties)` |
| **Create** | External provider | 1 | Service | `engine.resolveCreate(...)` |
| **Read** | Repository (internal) | 1 | Repository | `engine.resolveRead(roles, entity, subjects)` |
| **Update** | Repository (internal) | 2 | Service (gate 1+2 collapsed) | `repo.findByIdForAllow(id, accessContext)` → boolean |
| **Update** | External provider | 2 | Service (gate 1+2 collapsed) | `repo.findByIdForAllow(id, accessContext)` → boolean |
| **Delete** (id only) | Repository / external | 2 | Service | `repo.findByIdForAllow(id, accessContext)` → boolean |
| **Delete** (row in hand) | Repository / external | 1 | Service | `engine.resolveDelete(roles, entity, subjects, rowProperties)` |

reference.statement: There is no `Read / external provider` row: external providers are write-only in this architecture; reads always end at the repository.

claims.text: `candidateProperties` come from the validated request body. Untrusted ids inside those properties remain a vulnerability surface — same as any input, validate before passing.

reference.statement: **Why one gate.** The candidate row's properties are what the caller is about to write. Authorization is a pure function of `(effectiveRoles, subjects, properties)` — no DB lookup needed.

claims.text: `where` may be `undefined` (allow all rows). When no role grants read, `where` evaluates to `1 = 0` and `select` is empty — the query returns zero rows naturally without special-casing.
The service layer for reads is a thin pass-through. No service-side switch is needed.

reference.statement: **Why one gate, and why at the repo.** The engine's `where` / `joins` / `select` IS the result narrowing — it must be applied at the SQL boundary, not at the service.

snippets.caption: ts

claims.text: `findByIdForAllow` is the canonical name and the canonical contract: "does the engine's update filter, applied to the user's effective roles, include this id?" It returns `boolean`. It does **not** mutate. It does **not** return the row contents. Returning `boolean` keeps gate 2 unable to leak data when gate 1 has already approved the role.

snippets.code:
GATE 1 (service)     role check: is any rule potentially applicable?
   ↓ if allow
findByIdForAllow      repo lookup: is THIS row inside the engine's WHERE for update?
   ↓ if returns true
GATE 2 (service)      execute the update via repo OR external provider

reference.statement: **Why two gates.** Update rules typically reference fields the caller does not have at hand — e.g. `entity.workspaceId:$session.activeWorkspaceId` requires reading the row's `workspaceId` from storage. The decision cannot come from the request body alone.

claims.text: **Variant A — caller has only the id.** Identical to update.
**Variant B — caller has the row already (or a reliable identifier subset).** If the row is already loaded for unrelated reasons, pass its properties to `resolveDelete` directly.

**When to choose each:** Variant A is the default. Variant B is an optimization when the row is already in hand. **Do not** fetch the row solely to use Variant B — if you must call the DB anyway, use Variant A and keep gate 2 explicit.

reference.statement: Two flavors, chosen by what the caller already has.

claims.text: Logs go to the **audit channel** (typically `logger.child({ channel: "audit" })`), not the diagnostic logger. Audit logs may be retained for compliance; diagnostic logs may not.
Reads typically do not log per-row; they may log aggregate access events at the route boundary.

reference.statement: Every gate that produces a decision must be logged before the throw:

imagesAndDiagrams.value:
| Field | Required | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `userId` | yes | Who asked |
| `activeOrgId` (or equivalent tenant key) | yes | Where they asked |
| `entity` | yes | What kind of thing |
| `action` | yes | `read` / `create` / `update` / `delete` |
| `decision` | yes | `"allowed"` or `"denied"` |
| `effectiveRoles` | yes | What roles produced the decision |
| `targetIds` | for update / delete | The row id |
| `properties` | for create only | The candidate row's properties (validate before logging — never log secrets) |

reference.topic: Reference › Field-level write gating — known gap
reference.statement: Today the engine evaluates target scopes against `properties` for writes but does not narrow the *writable column set* against the role's `fields` allowlist. Until that is implemented, treat field-level write authorization as a **TODO at the service layer** — between the verdict and the executor — using the same `fields` array the role declares. Document such checks inline so they migrate cleanly when the engine surfaces this natively.

claims.text: **Repository re-resolves on writes.** Write repos must NOT call `engine.resolveCreate/Update/Delete` themselves. The service makes the verdict; the repo only executes. (Read repos call `engine.resolveRead` because narrowing IS the result.)
**Service skips `findByIdForAllow` and trusts the id from the request body for update/delete.** Gate 2 is mandatory unless variant B applies.
**Service trusts client-supplied properties for create.** Validate properties via the same mechanism as any other request input before passing to `resolveCreate`.
**Repository returns the row from `findByIdForAllow`.** It returns `boolean` only. The next step's executor fetches the row by id if needed.
**Skipping the audit log on a deny.** A deny is the security-relevant event; not logging it loses the trail.
**Hand-rolling a role check anywhere in the codebase.** Authorization is the engine's job — re-implementing it bypasses the rules and is the most common source of permission bugs.
